data.title: The Oral GLP-1 Tracker: Wegovy pill, Foundayo both grow
data.description:
With the recent launches of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly’s Foundayo, the obesity market has started to shift toward oral GLP-1 drugs. While Novo leverages its first-mover advantage with the familiar Wegovy brand, Lilly is betting that the freedom from strict fasting and water requirements can give Foundayo an edge.

Each week, Fierce Pharma’s Oral GLP-1 Tracker will leverage analysts’ notes and IQVIA data to monitor prescription trends and shifting market shares as these two titans vie to become the go-to oral weight-loss solution for millions.

UPDATED: Sept. 4, 2026

Total prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo both grew over the past week, reaching roughly 181K (+3%) and 44K (+8%), IQVIA data showed, as cited by Citi. Both numbers are the two meds' highest so far. 

While Foundayo has yet to catch up with Wegovy pill, the market share gap between the two oral drugs is slowly narrowing. According to an Aug. 28 Jefferies note based on data the previous week, Foundayo's share of new prescriptions (NRx), which exclude refills, was 21.5% in the oral obesity market.

Back to the most recent week, Wegovy pill's position within the Wegovy family remained stable at 35%, as total Wegovy scripts increased 2.7% sequentially to 513.5K. During the same period, Lilly's Zepbound scripts climbed 1.6% to a little fewer than 772K.  

UPDATE: Aug. 28, 2026

Twenty weeks into its launch, Eli Lilly's Foundayo has finally exceeded 40,000 in weekly prescriptions, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 drug posted 40,862 scripts last week, bouncing back from a small dip the week prior. Still, the drug's scripts level is no match for the roughly 57K that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill garnered at week 6 of its own launch.

In its 33rd week of launch, the Wegovy pill booked roughly 175K scripts, slightly down from 176K, per IQVIA. The share of the oral version of semaglutide in all Wegovy obesity scripts was flat week over week at 35%. All told, across the pill and the injectable, Wegovy's weekly scripts were a little over 500K, down 0.8% sequentially.

As Jefferies analysts observed in an Aug. 21 note, Wegovy has been relatively flat since the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program began July 1.

Overall, the roughly 60%-40% obesity market share split between Lilly and Novo remained stable, as Lilly's Zepbound held its ground as the most popular drug.

UPDATE: Aug. 21, 2026

After a one-week hiccup, Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill regained its momentum last week with its largest prescription rate since it was launched in January. There were more than 176,000 prescriptions for the pill in the period, according to data gathered by IQVIA and cited in a note by Citi. 

The oral treatment now accounts for 35% of total Wegovy prescriptions, which is up from 33% the previous week, analysts from Citi said in their weekly update to investors.

Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo, which had been on a steady five-week climb, backtracked, with a drop-off from 38,928 prescriptions in the prior period to 36,620 in the latest week.

The movements for the two oral treatments contributed to overall market share adjustments for the companies' diabetes and obesity medicines. While Lilly made a 0.1% gain to 56.7%, Novo increased its market share by 0.3% to 37.1%.  

UPDATE: Aug. 14, 2026

Despite its leading position in the oral GLP-1 market, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill seems to be hitting a market share ceiling. For months now, shares of total prescriptions for Wegovy pill within the entire Wegovy franchise have struggled to break through the one-third mark.

While share of oral semaglutide within all Wegovy scripts hit 35% in our previous update, it fell back to 33% last week, as Wegovy pill scripts dropped to about 163K, down from a high of roughly 172K the week prior, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

Total Wegovy scripts, including the original injectable, declined 1.1% sequentially to about 495.5K. As a result, Novo yielded about 0.7 percentage point in obesity market share to Eli Lilly's Zepbound last week based on the IQVIA data. The split stood at 39.9% and 60.1% between Novo and Lilly.

Meanwhile, Lilly's Foundayo continued its upward trajectory with 38,928 total scripts, representing another step up from its previous record of 34,219 set the week prior.

UPDATE: Aug. 7, 2026

Prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo continue to build, jumping 16% sequentially to 34,219 the previous week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The oral GLP-1 med has been on a roll lately as it appears to celebrate four weeks of consecutive growth in total scripts. However, as Citi noted, there's still a potential gap in IQVIA's capture of telehealth data, and it's not clear how much of the scripts growth was from IQVIA getting better at including those data, or, if the actual growth was much faster in telehealth channels.

This week, Lilly's reported Foundayo sales for the second quarter—$98 million in total, including $67 million in the U.S.—disappointed many. As CEO David Ricks noted on an earnings call, Lilly began broad direct-to-consumer marketing to raise consumer awareness after securing commercial access across the three major pharmacy benefit managers in June. Besides, The Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program went live on July 1, offering coverage for certain weight-loss medications, including Foundayo, for a $50 copayment per month. Ilya Yuffa, president of Lilly USA and global customer capabilities, said the company is "starting to see an inflection point on Foundayo now."

As for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill, total scripts recorded by IQVIA have been largely flat with small upticks in the past two weeks, having reached roughly 172K in the previous week. The oral version of semaglutide now makes up 35% of total Wegovy scripts, which take up about 40.6% of the U.S. obesity market share, as Lilly's Zepbound remains the leader. 

UPDATE: July 31, 2026

The small inflection point we noticed two weeks ago regarding Eli Lilly's Foundayo does not appear to be a flash in the pan. Weekly total prescriptions for the small molecule reached 29,388, a new high for the oral GLP-1 receptor agonist after three weeks of consecutive growth, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. 

As IQVIA may be missing some scripts from telehealth channels, we will get a clearer picture of Foundayo's launch progress when Lilly reports its second-quarter earnings on Wednesday, Aug. 5. Analysts at Jefferies have been modeling $71 million in U.S. sales for the quarter based on IQVIA data.

Meanwhile, Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill remains far ahead in the oral GLP-1 race with total scripts also hitting a new record of about 171,700, according to Citi. The number represents 1.1% growth from its previous best recorded during the prior week.

Coincidentally, the entire GLP-1 class also saw its total scripts grow 1.1% sequentially across diabetes and obesity uses. Lilly's Zepbound regained some lost ground with total scripts up 1.9% week over week. That's compared to Wegovy, which now makes up 40.6% of the obesity market after a 0.2% sequential decline in total scripts. 

Novo reports earnings on the same day as Lilly, Aug. 5.

UPDATE: July 24, 2026

After a post-holiday lull, prescriptions for GLP-1s have more than bounced back. Weekly prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo reached new highs during the previous week, collecting 169,800 and 26,760, respectively, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. The two oral drugs' previous records were about 161.5K and 24.3K, respectively. 

Other GLP-1 drugs also enjoyed a boost, as total GLP-1 scripts across obesity and diabetes increased 6.6% sequentially, according to Citi.

From the obesity front, scripts for Lilly's Zepbound rose 7.7% sequentially to about 710K. The GLP-1/GIP dual agonist conceded 0.6 percentage points of market share to Novo but remains ahead of the game with a 58.9% share. That's compared to a 10.5% week-over-week scripts expansion for Novo's Wegovy, which mounted to about 495.5K. In that basket, about 34% belonged to Wegovy pill.

UPDATE: July 17, 2026

Following the Independence Day holiday, the overall GLP-1 market was down 5.1% week over week as measured by total prescriptions across obesity and diabetes uses, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi.

In the obesity field specifically, total scripts for Eli Lilly's Zepbound shrank by 3.1% sequentially to a little below 660K, while Novo Nordisk's Wegovy dipped 4.4% to about 448.5K.

Against this backdrop, Lilly's oral Foundayo seemed to enjoy a small inflection point, with a total 24,303 scripts notably breaking away from its roughly 20K level in the prior five weeks.  

Meanwhile, joining the bigger trend, Wegovy pill scripts dropped to 147.5K during the week, versus about 153K the prior week or 161.5K at its peak. But the contribution of the oral version to the overall Wegovy scripts remained stable at around a third, per Citi's note. 

UPDATE: July 10, 2026

The launch of Eli Lilly’s Foundayo remains “muted,” with weekly prescriptions flat over the last five weeks, analysts from Jefferies said in a July 10 note. The analysis is based on data collected by IQVIA.

In the 13th week of Foundayo’s launch, IQVIA reported 19,550 prescriptions, down for the third straight week after peaking at Week 10 with 21,648 prescriptions. The figure also comes in significantly shy of the Week 13 launch of Novo’s Wegovy pill (more than 105K scripts) and Lilly’s injected obesity treatment Zepbound (59K), but ahead of Novo’s injected Wegovy (13K).

Meanwhile, weekly scripts for Wegovy pill ticked slightly upward sequentially to about 153K, although they still lag behind the drug’s peak of more than 161K.

Jefferies points out that CVS was the last of the big three PBMs to provide coverage of Foundayo, starting on June 1. By contrast, Wegovy had full coverage at the first week of its launch.

While Jefferies’ $71 million quarterly sales projection for Foundayo sits significantly below Wall Street consensus of $130 million, the team still believes that the Lilly med can reach the consensus revenue estimate of $1.2 billion for 2026.

UPDATE: July 6, 2026

For a month now, weekly prescriptions for Eli Lilly's Foundayo have been hovering at around 20,000. In other words, three months into its market debut, the non-peptide GLP-1 receptor agonist was still at the same script level that Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill had achieved in two to three weeks post-launch.

For the week ended on June 26, Foundayo's total scripts dipped about 4% sequentially to 19,830, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. During the same period, scripts were also down about 2% for oral Wegovy, reaching about 149,000.

In a July 4 report, Jefferies analysts modeled about $71 million in U.S. sales during Foundayo's debut quarter from April to June, versus the team's previous estimate of $85 million in a June 26 report. Wall Street's consensus currently has the number at $130 million. To reach its estimate, Jefferies used an illustrative calculation based on the IQVIA data, with certain assumptions regarding pricing, dosing and stocking.

While Lilly still lags Novo on the oral GLP-1 battlefield, the Indianapolis pharma has maintained a majority 59.5% share of the overall obesity market, according to IQVIA's prescription data.  

As Novo's injectable Wegovy gained about 0.2% scripts (roughly 500) to reach 315,000 for the period, Lilly's Zepbound expanded by 1%, including 375,000 (+3,500) from Zepbound autoinjector and 289,000 (+2,000) from Zepbound DTC Vial+KwikPen.

UPDATE: June 29, 2026

Likely thanks to the Juneteenth federal holiday, prescriptions for both Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill and Eli Lilly's Foundayo were lower compared with their highest. For the week ended on June 19, Foundayo logged 20,594 total scripts, down from 21,648 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Jefferies. 

For oral Wegovy, the numbers were about 152,000 for the June 19 week, a roughly 9,500 (5.9%) decrease from the prior week. 

As Jefferies' analysts noted, most GLP-1 scripts were down or rather flat in their weekly comparisons. Injectable Wegovy added about 1,000 (0.3%) scripts, landing at 315,000. Mounjaro essentially saw no change, at 804,000.

Lilly has previously noted that it takes time to build awareness for Foundayo as a new brand, whereas Novo benefits from familiarity with the Wegovy moniker. 

Meanwhile, Sandoz just announced that the FDA has accepted its generic tirzepatide autoinjector applications, covering all indications of Lilly's Mounjaro and Zepbound. We'll see how the availability of a generic injectable version shakes up the oral market. 

UPDATE: June 18, 2026

Name recognition and "familiarity" with Novo Nordisk's oral Wegovy has contributed to its rapid uptake in its battle with Lilly's oral GLP-1 Foundayo, according to Spherix analyst Jim Hickey, who conducts monthly surveys with doctors who prescribe the treatments. See Fierce's story on Hickey's analysis here.

UPDATE: June 12, 2026

The share of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy pill among total Wegovy scripts appears to have reached a plateau, hovering around one-third over the past few weeks. The latest number for the week ended on June 5 was 33%, compared with 30%, 32% and 31% in the prior weeks, according to Citi. 

Meanwhile, the obesity market share split between Wegovy and Eli Lilly's Zepbound has been relatively stable at around 40% to 42%, as the Indianapolis pharma's oral Foundayo makes up only a small portion of the market even though its own scripts continue to build. 

Wegovy's total scripts were up 9.8% on a weekly basis, reaching nearly 484,500. Within this haul, Wegovy pill contributed roughly 159,000, the oral version's highest since its launch. The drug's previous highest was 146,000 before dipping to 134,000 in our last update.

Zepbound's scripts also grew week over week by 9.3%, nearing 667,400 for the week. During the same period, IQVIA tracked slightly shy of 20,000 scripts from Foundayo in its ninth week on the market, compared with nearly 17,000 the prior week. 

Thanks to the expansion of the oral version, Wegovy overall now commands 42.1% of the obesity market. Tracing backwards, its share has been climbing steadily, clocking in at 41.9%, 41.2%, 41.4%, 40.5%, 40.4%, 42.6% and 40.4% in the past few weeks.

UPDATE: June 8, 2026

It took just over five months for Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill to log 3 million total U.S. prescriptions, underscoring “one of the strongest US pharmaceutical launches by volume on record,” the company announced in a June 7 press release. Meanwhile, Eli Lilly’s rival Foundayo has still yet to achieve more than 17,000 prescriptions, according to a June 5 note from Citi analysts.  

Using data from IQVIA, the analysts tracked 16,982 Foundayo prescriptions as of the drug's eighth week on the market since its April launch. However, the Citi team emphasizes that “there may be a gap in telehealth capture,” as Lilly has previously confirmed to the analysts around 20,000 Foundayo scripts since its launch. Foundayo has been floating around this range for several weeks now since hitting 16,698 at week six, the data show.

Meanwhile, Novo’s Wegovy pill was at 73,544 prescriptions by the time it had hit the same eight-week marker in its own launch. The drug had picked up one million prescriptions 12 weeks after launching and nabbed an additional two million prescriptions in the following ten weeks, Novo said in its release. At its three million total, one prescription is filled roughly every five seconds, the company pointed out in its release. 

Either way, IQVIA’s data suggests a preference for oral formulations in the wider GLP-1 market, with oral Wegovy prescriptions now contributing 30% of total Wegovy scripts, according to the Citi analysts. The oral offering may be driving a wider market for the obesity treatments as well, with Novo explaining in its recent release that more than 80% of its new prescriptions for the Wegovy pill come from people new to GLP-1 therapy. 

June 2 findings from Spherix Global Insights second the notion that oral GLP-1 pills are expanding the overall treatment pool and drawing in a “massive wave of new patients,” the company said in an emailed release. In oral Wegovy’s first four weeks on the market earlier this year, 73% of surveyed primary care physician reported prescribing the med, with over 98% who haven’t yet prescribed it planning to within the next six months, Spherix found. 

“Novo Nordisk’s early performance has set an exceptionally high bar for the competition,” Spherix’s gastroenterology franchise head, Jim Hickey, commented.

On a weekly basis, however, total GLP-1 prescriptions were trending downward over the week of June 1, falling 5.7% week-over-week, Citi analysts noted. Other than the continued rollout of Lilly and Novo’s respective weight loss pills, the analysts cited the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies as a key future event that they think could impact total prescriptions. 

UPDATE: June 1, 2026

In its seventh week on the market, which ended May 22, Eli Lilly’s obesity pill Foundayo continued to track below the pace of Novo Nordisk’s rival Wegovy pill at the same point in its launch.

At the same time, analysts at Jefferies and Citi again flagged caveats that could be skewing the numbers, with the Jefferies team espousing confidence that Lilly’s oral GLP-1 can still meet consensus sales projections for both the second quarter and 2026 as a whole. 

Breaking down the numbers, the Jefferies team put seventh-week total Foundayo prescriptions lower versus the previous week at roughly 11,700, with the clarification that the data’s source, IQVIA, had to use a “best-estimate” tally for the latest week’s prescription trends. 

That trend remains “numerically lower” than the course charted by Novo’s Wegovy pill, which racked up an impressive 67,000 prescriptions in its seventh week, although Foundayo’s performance still tracks ahead of Novo’s injectable Wegovy and Lilly’s first obesity incretin med Zepbound at the same point in their respective rollouts, the analyst team said. 

Lilly has suggested it expects the market for oral obesity meds to “develop over time” and has also cited the time needed to build new brand awareness for Foundayo, according to Jefferies, which added that the Lilly pill’s commercial reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly” compared to oral Wegovy. Lilly has confirmed that coverage of Foundayo through CVS Caremark, the United States’ biggest PBM, will begin this week. 

Despite those apparent growing pains, the analysts at Jefferies called Foundayo’s ability to meet consensus sales estimates in the near-term and for the full year as “doable.” The analysts currently predict that Lilly’s oral weight loss med will garner $145 million in the second quarter on the way to a $1.6 billion haul for the full year. 

Consensus estimates are tracking for Q2 and full-year Foundayo sales of $136 million and $1.2 billion, respectively, according to Jefferies. 

On that note, analysts at Citi, have repeatedly warned that IQVIA’s prescription data may be failing to account for telehealth referrals, citing comments from Lilly executives on the total patients they were tracking as of the company’s Q1 earnings call. For its part, Citi placed the total number of Foundayo scripts for the week ending May 22 at roughly 16,000, based on the IQVIA stats. 

By comparison, Novo’s Wegovy pill clocked some 146,000 total scripts over that same seven-day stretch, per Citi. Citi once more flagged that Novo’s Wegovy pill is making up a growing portion of overall semaglutide obesity prescriptions, which the team said points to “preferences for oral formulations.”

UPDATE: May 22, 2026

With both Novo Nordisk’s and Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1s establishing their footing in the U.S. obesity market, the companies’ respective Wegovy pill and orforglipron tablet Foundayo are making their mark on prescription trends for a class previously confined primarily to injectables.

Looking at the past four weeks, total U.S. GLP-1 prescriptions were up 3.6%, compared to 1.8% at the same time last year, analysts at Citi wrote in a Friday note to clients, citing script tracking data from IQVIA. The Citi team attributed that momentum to the ability of Novo’s and Lilly’s new oral launches to “broaden and reshape the market” for obesity incretin drugs.

As of the week ended May 15, IQVIA logged nearly 17,000 prescriptions for Lilly’s Foundayo, which debuted on April 9. As in prior weeks, the Citi analysts caveated that IQVIA’s data may be missing key prescribing stats from telehealth channels, flagging Lilly executives’ comments during an earnings call at the end of last month that there were then roughly 20,000 patients on the new oral therapy.

Conversely, Novo’s Wegovy pill has recorded roughly 142,000 prescriptions as of last week, according to Citi’s note.

In an apparent sign of the new oral option's popularity, the analysts flagged that oral Wegovy now comprises 31% of total prescriptions for the brand, which is otherwise administered as an injection. The Citi team noted that this trend could signal “preferences for oral formulations.”

Meanwhile, scoping out the broader U.S. GLP-1 market over the past four weeks, Lilly’s tirzepatide brand—which includes both Zepbound for obesity and Mounjaro for Type 2 diabetes—now holds a 54.8% share compared to a 47% piece of the pie last year. Novo’s U.S. market share for semaglutide has remained “relatively flat” over that stretch and clocked in at 37.4%, per Citi.

Week over week, total GLP-1 prescriptions were down a little less than 1% in the U.S. Looking at obesity specifically, Citi’s analysts flagged a 2.1% tirzepatide prescription decline versus last week, while Novo’s Wegovy prescriptions tracked at a positive 1.8%.

Aside from both companies' oral GLP-1 launches continuing to add texture to the market, the analysts noted that the effect of the Trump administration’s “most favored nation” pricing policies on Novo’s and Lilly’s drugs could boost overall prescriptions for the class. 

UPDATE: May 15, 2026

Total prescriptions for Eli Lilly’s Foundayo reached 10,248 for the week that ended May 8, up from 7,335 the prior week, according to IQVIA data cited by Citi. While still on the rise, Foundayo’s growth pace continued to lag behind that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill during the same stage of their launch. 

Wegovy’s total scripts rose by 1.3% week over week to nearly 446,000, as its share in the obesity GLP-1 market climbed 0.1 percentage point to 40.5%, according to Citi.

However, Wegovy’s growth apparently didn’t come from its oral formulation. Wegovy pill scripts landed at about 137,000 for the week, down from roughly 143,000 the prior week, marking the first time that the pill's scripts have fallen since the oral launch in early January.

Scripts from the Wegovy pill made up 31% of total Wegovy scripts for the period, down 2 percentage points from the previous week. Still, Citi analysts argued that this roughly one-third of share “suggests preferences for oral formulations.”

Even as Wegovy gained ground, Lilly’s Zepbound remained the obesity market leader, with 59.5% share, as its nearly 656,000 scripts marked 0.8% growth week over week. 

UPDATE: May 8, 2026

As Eli Lilly’s Foundayo finds its footing on the market, Novo Nordisk’s own Wegovy pill—which got a three-month head start to launch over its rival this year—is starting to illuminate just how significant an oral GLP-1 may be to the lucrative obesity drug landscape. 

In the fourth week since its April 9 debut in the U.S., Lilly’s Foundayo has generated 7,335 total prescriptions, analysts at Citi wrote in a note to clients Friday, citing prescribing stats from IQVIA. 

That ramp-up looks slower on paper than that enjoyed by the Wegovy pill during its initial rollout, but the Citi team cautioned that there may be a gap in IQVIA data linked to telehealth prescriptions for Lilly’s tablet. They pointed to comments from Lilly executives late last week indicating that there were now some 20,000 patients on Foundayo, with the company noting that telehealth platforms were generating some 35% of the oral GLP-1 medicine’s current launch volume. 

The analysts acknowledged that Lilly’s early Foundayo prescription trends “continue to build,” while adding that they “look for further growth to develop the oral competitive market.” 

During its earnings call last week, Lilly added that upcoming coverage secured at major pharmacy benefit managers should come online by the middle of May, providing a likely sizeable tailwind to Foundayo’s trajectory. 

As for Novo, the company logged some 440,410 Wegovy prescriptions on the week that ended May 1, with oral Wegovy now making up 33% of those total obesity referrals, per the Citi analysts, who said that trend could reflect “preferences for oral formulations.”

The update on the oral obesity numbers comes after Novo earlier this week reported that the Wegovy pill generated 2.26 billion Danish kroner (around $355 million) in its first quarter on the U.S. market. 

For its part, Foundayo will likely need to start generating around 22,000 prescriptions a week in order to hit current consensus forecasts of $160 million in second-quarter sales, RBC Capital Markets’ Trung ​Huynh said this week, as cited by Reuters. 

UPDATE: May 4, 2026

With three weeks of data on Lilly’s oral GLP-1 launch in obesity now on the books, the dimensions of Foundayo’s rollout—and its critical comparison to that of Novo Nordisk’s Wegovy pill—are coming into focus. 

In its third week on the U.S. market, which ended April 24, Foundayo generated some 5,600 prescriptions, analysts at Jefferies wrote in a May 1 note to clients. That level of adoption is numerically lower than the stats recorded by the Wegovy pill in its third week, when prescriptions for the oral obesity med came in at around 26,100, per the note. 

Nevertheless, almost all of Foundayo’s recorded performance stems from cash pay channels, according to the Jefferies team, with commercial access via insurance set to come online by the middle of this month, which will likely give Foundayo a substantial boost in uptake. 

The team acknowledged that Foundayo’s reimbursement “appears to be ramping more slowly vs oral Wegovy’s.” 

Overall, the analysts described Foundayo as “off to a solid start,” and estimate the drug will generate $146 million in the second quarter and $1.6 billion for all of 2026. That compares to consensus forecasts of $134 million and $1.2 billion, respectively. 

Lilly told the Jefferies team that, as of week three of its launch, some 45% of Foundayo prescriptions were coming through its direct-to-patient channel LillyDirect, alongside 35% of referrals from telehealth providers and the remaining 20% coming from traditional retail venues. 

During an earnings call with analysts last week, Lilly executives noted that there were around 20,000 patients on Foundayo in the U.S. The drug was approved April 1. 

As for Novo’s pill, oral Wegovy lassoed around 135,000 total prescriptions during the week that ended April 24, according to the Jefferies notes. 

UPDATE: April 24, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 obesity treatment Foundayo has attracted 3,707 prescriptions though its second week on the market, lagging far behind the pace of Novo Nordisk’s GLP-1 pill Wegovy, which drew 18,410 prescriptions though its second week on the market in January. 

The results were made available by Jefferies from healthcare analytics firm IQVIA and are good through the week ending on April 17.

With the result, Lilly’s shares dipped by 4% on Friday, compared to a 7% gain for Novo.

Foundayo’s launch so far does compare favorably to that of Novo’s injected Wegovy, which numbered 1,578 prescriptions through two weeks when it reached the market in the U.S. but falls short of Lilly’s Zepbound pen, which counted 7,292 prescriptions through its second week.

In its note to investors, analysts from Jefferies called the result “disappointing vs. expectations."

Brand recognition has played a role, according to Bernstein analyst Courtney Breen, who said that online searches for GLP-1 drugs peaked during Wegovy’s launch, potentially boosting demand.

UPDATE: April 21, 2026

Eli Lilly’s oral GLP-1 Foundayo is off to a solid launch, drawing 1,390 prescriptions in its first week on the market, according to tracking figures from IQVIA and presented by Jefferies. The tabulation is from the week starting April 6. This compares to the 3,071 prescriptions Novo Nordisk garnered during its Wegovy pill launch week in January.

While Foundayo came up short in this oral GLP-1 launch week comparison, it did exceed the number of prescriptions recorded in the first week of the launch of both Lilly’s injected Zepbound (1,100) and Novo’s injected version of Wegovy (768).

In a note to clients, analysts with Jefferies cautioned that comparisons can be “tricky” given that oral Wegovy was launched at the start of the year and that initial capture rates from IQVIA are “volatile” and may not include product sampling. 

“Overall, we think Foundayo’s initial scripts look excellent,” the Jefferies team wrote, adding that it is modeling Foundayo’s sales to reach $1.6 billion this year, compared to a consensus of $1.5 billion, with its peak annual sales topping out at $30 billion versus the consensus of $26 billion. 

“We think the real opportunity for Foundayo is ex-U.S., given its clear advantages on scale, distribution and [cost of goods sold],” Jefferies wrote.

data.title: UCB’s Bimzelx claims August’s top pharma ad spending spot
data.description:
Move over AbbVie and Johnson & Johnson, we have a new and surprising leading drug in the pharma ad spending space.

According to data from iSpot.TV, UCB’s immunology drug Bimzelx jumped 17 positions month-over-month to claim the top spot as the highest pharma drug ad spend in August.

This is the first time UCB’s med has ever taken the lead with a meaty $31.5 million in spend, up from the $5.5 million the company spent in July. 

This pushed AbbVie’s rival immunology therapy Skyrizi into second place, though spend was only fractionally lower at $30.3 million. Skyrizi had taken the top spot in July. 

Related

AbbVie’s Skyrizi retakes edge in pharma’s July ad spending league

J&J’s Tremfya, also an immunology med that rivals Bimzelx and Skyrizi, was down one spot in August to third, with AbbVie’s second major immunology drug Rinvoq coming in fourth place. 

Spending difference between the two was marginal, with Tremfya seeing $25.6 million channeled into its commercials last month, and Rinvoq’ spend just $300,000 lower. 

In fifth and sixth positions was J&J again, this time with its atypical antipsychotic drug Caplyta, down two places from July, while the U.S. Big Pharma’s newly launched psoriasis drug Icotyde continued its swift push into a regular top 10 spot to reach sixth place. 

Merck’s megablockbuster oncology drug Keytruda, an unusual medicine for these lists, remained in the top 10 for a second month, though down two spots from July in seventh. 

Sanofi and Regeneron’s immunology drug Dupixent, meanwhile, jumped two places to reach eighth, while Boehringer Ingelheim and Eli Lilly’s diabetes, kidney disease and CV drug Jardiance was ninth. 

AbbVie’s neurology drug took the final tenth spot, up four places from July with a spend of $10.1 million. 

Check out the top 10 below. 

 

1. Bimzelx

Movement: Up seventeen spots

What is it? UCB’s immunology drug

Est. national linear TV ad spend: $31.2 million (up from $5.5 million in July) 

  • Hidradenitis suppurativa: $11.8 million 
  • Psoriasis: $10.8 million

data.title: How DOLs Are Reshaping Prescribing — And How Pharma Can Help
data.description:
Clinical protocols often fail to keep pace with the latest research. On average, it takes 17 years for new evidence to become standard clinical practice.

In the meantime, 61% of physicians regularly scan social media to understand where science is heading, and 57% say it has already changed their view of medication. A single digital opinion leader (DOL) with millions of followers can influence the prescribing decisions of thousands of HCPs.

By providing DOLs with timely, evidence-based content, pharma has an opportunity to help shape the narratives reaching this audience. The key point is that life sciences brands don’t need to persuade HCPs to engage with DOLs. They are already listening.
 

Why HCPs Turn to DOLs


HCPs have a legitimate reason to follow DOLs: their patients are becoming more curious and increasingly turning to AI-powered search for answers. Faced with a new diagnosis, many are eager to find reassuring explanations and may trust inaccurate, oversimplified AI responses that reinforce their own hopes and biases.

That leaves physicians responsible for correcting misinformation while delivering care. Timely, medically governed insights from trusted DOLs help them stay on top of the latest evidence and conversations happening online.
 

Finding the Right DOLs Is an Uphill Climb


Pharma teams lack a structured approach to finding the right DOLs for their campaigns. They often pay attention to a DOL's visibility, mistaking it for influence. 

Yet, the process should begin with a clear understanding of campaign objectives, market dynamics, target audience, and therapeutic focus before creating a shortlist of potential collaborators.
 


Every DOL should be evaluated against clear eligibility criteria (5Rs). Without a strong "resume" (scientific credibility), resonance, relevance, reach, and reliability, brands risk investing in partnerships that won't deliver the outcomes they set out to achieve.

However, meeting all these criteria is easier said than done. Some respected traditional Key Opinion Leaders (KOLs) have little or no digital presence. Some highly visible creators have influence but are not HCPs. Others are active online but rarely discuss the relevant therapeutic area, while some have large audiences that fall outside the target segment. And even candidates who seem like a good fit may publish content that lacks scientific rigor or poses compliance risks.

So, when you find and score your DOLs, the next step is to prioritize them. The score is important, but it is not the only factor. Teams should also consider whether the DOL fits local market goals, whether a partnership is realistic, and whether they have the time and resources to support it. 
 

Like Any Relationship, DOL Relationships Need Nurturing


Finding the right DOL is only one piece of the puzzle. The next step is activating those relationships. The right DOLs already have the audience, clinical credibility, and motivation to communicate evidence accurately. What they often lack is the time and tools to create content consistently and respond in real time. 

In practice, that means providing post ideas, pre-approved content kits, and evidence-backed assets they can quickly adapt and share. One way to give a DOL something usable on their timeline is to have the building blocks approved and waiting: modular claims organized by therapeutic area, platform-specific templates, and a clear line back to the approved source for every piece, so both the DOL and the company stay protected.

Finally, resist the temptation to hide promotional intent and be clear about why you’re collaborating. The conversation should be framed as: “We are here to help you share timely, evidence-based information with the HCPs who trust your expertise.”
 

DOL Engagement Is a Work in Progress


Engaging DOLs is always a continious effort. As Mark Watson, co-founder of Fractal Force, said on the Pharma Talks podcast: “A brand plan and HCP personas are useful, but effective physician engagement depends on understanding what HCPs are thinking right now and what they need today. That is what a real conversation looks like.” 

Track audience signals, disease focus, and HCP responses over time. These insights help ensure you’re speaking the same language as your audience when the rubber meets the road.

Monitor posting frequency, audience growth, therapeutic focus, engagement patterns, and changes in content quality or scientific consistency. At the same time, watch for shifts in audience demographics, geography, or compliance risks that may require re-prioritization.
 

The US Market Moment and Why 2026 is the Right Time to Move


The US is home to one of the world’s most active communities of physicians on platforms like LinkedIn, YouTube, and X. A recent survey of 150 US clinicians found that many use social media to stay aware of new therapies, while podcasts and video content have become common sources of professional education. 

At the same time, the US pharma market is highly competitive, with multiple juggernauts competing within the same therapeutic area. When products offer comparable efficacy and safety profiles, pharma teams must invest more heavily in building awareness and educating physicians early in the adoption journey. 

Just as the need to educate physicians has grown, access to them has declined. HCP access in the US has fallen from 60% to 45% in recent years due to rising patient volumes, healthcare consolidation, and tighter health system restrictions. With fewer opportunities for in-person engagement, leading brands started to rely on DOLs, helping physicians interpret new evidence, apply it in clinical practice, and counter misinformation online.
 

Start With the Rules Instead of Search


Before you start searching for DOLs, define the rules of the game. Clarify your objective, target audience, therapy area, market, and preferred digital channels. Those decisions determine who qualifies as a relevant DOL and who simply has a large following. 

In practice, the most difficult part is verification. Establish clear criteria around scientific credibility, clinical relevance, reach, reliability, and audience resonance. 

And remember: DOLs, social media, market, HCPs, and science are changing over time, so successful programs are always built for long-term monitoring. 

The conversation shaping how HCPs think about your therapeutic area is happening either way. The only question is whether pharma's evidence is part of it. 

At Viseven, we help brands make sure it is by finding, validating, engaging, and monitoring the DOLs who matter most. If you're exploring DOL engagement and would like a hand, reach out.

data.title: Novartis teams with Olympian Laviai Nielsen on MS campaign
data.description:
Novartis is taking social media by storm with a multiple sclerosis (MS) campaign that urges patients to #KnowYourMS, a message backed by British Olympian Laviai Nielsen. 

Throughout the summer, the company has been posting a blend of patient stories and short branded videos across its social channels to amplify its patient advocacy push in MS and inspire patients to bring up concerns about their condition with their doctors. The videos link to Novartis’ “you know your MS best” webpage, which has a stated goal of helping patients decide if it’s worth bringing up changes in their condition with their doctor. 

The page is full of resources that can help patients prepare for a doctor visit, including an MS checklist, workbook and questionnaire to help track symptom changes.

In Novartis’ branded videos for the campaign, women are depicted running into MS symptoms while going about their day, at work or with their family. In each clip, the woman stops and considers if the symptom is a change in her MS.

“Does doing things with your hands feel more difficult than it used to?” Novartis asks in the caption of one Instagram video. “Don’t push changes in your MS to the back of your mind. Start a conversation with your doctor today!” 

The messaging is further reinforced by Nielsen, who partnered with the company in an MS-focused social media collaboration. 

Nielsen, an Olympic bronze-winning sprinter, opens up about her MS in a series of collaborative Instagram posts that ran on both Novartis’ page and her own. The first video follows a popular online video format of “story time” videos, in which creators sit down in front of the camera to tell a personal story. 

Posted in July, Nielsen’s collaboration with Novartis fell on the fifth anniversary of her MS diagnosis, a story she says she hasn’t publicly shared until now. In the video, the athlete delves into the symptoms she experienced while racing at high-profile sporting events and explains how she went to physicians to push for an answer to her symptoms before finally receiving a diagnosis two days before she was scheduled to leave for the Tokyo Olympics in 2022. 

The video gives Novartis’ and Nielsen’s audience a real and personal look into her diagnosis journey, interspersing clips of her racing, waiting in the doctor’s office and images of her official diagnoses throughout.

“I wanted to share this story for anyone who’s living with MS or anyone who knows anyone who’s living with MS to listen to those subtle changes that are happening in your body,” she said. “You have a voice, and you can talk to your doctor and take that first step in moving forward.”

Nielsen and Novartis’ collaboration continued with other videos spread across both pages. In one, Nielsen shares “3 things I do differently since being diagnosed with MS.” In another more recent video, Nielsen discusses how “the best decisions come from honest conversations” and explains how she gets the best care by being open and honest about her condition with her healthcare team and her coach. 

Related

Genentech uncovers 'Hidden GeMS' in latest iteration of multiple sclerosis visibility drive

The posts, which all include “#ad” with Novartis in the captions, were well received by MS patients and supporters, who flooded the comments with encouragement and appreciation for her willingness to share her story.

Neilsen is one of several MS advocates Novartis has featured recently surrounding its global campaign urging patients to listen to their body’s warning signs and bring up potential concerns with a physician. Most recently, the company released a longer video featuring three patient advocates, who share anecdotes about experiencing subtle MS changes that led to drastic shifts over time. In each advocate’s self-filmed contribution, patients Andra, Ellen and Damian voice the same message, reminding others “you know your body.”

Novartis has historically showcased MS patients’ voices in its advocacy efforts and notes on its MS webpage that it sees patient groups as a “key partner in our decision-making.” The company further points out that it has been at the forefront of several groundbreaking MS innovations over the last decade, including producing the first oral disease-modifying therapy over a decade ago and most recently making the only self-administered targeted B-cell therapy, Kesimpta, in 2020.  

Just this week, Novartis made another splash in the MS scene with a pair of phase 3 wins for its BTK inhibitor Rhapsido, besting Sanofi’s older Aubagio at reducing annualized relapse rate in relapsing MS. The company now plans to file for global regulatory approval of the drug in MS, an indication that would join its initial 2025 approval in chronic spontaneous urticaria.

data.title: CMI forms new specialty communications business unit
data.description:
CMI Media Group is adding to its spread of media services through a new specialty communications business that introduces a slate of new cutting-edge marketing tools. 

The new business unit is centered on medical affairs, which CMI described as the industry’s essential “third pillar,” it explained in a Sept. 2 press release. By offering “high-value, insight-driven interactions” in the medical communications realm, the company figures it can improve patient outcomes and integrate therapeutic communications earlier in drug development. 

CMI is already working with “multiple leading biopharma organizations” to rework scientific exchanges based on its new breadth of services, it said. 

The core services wrapped into the specialty communications unit include "compliant omnichannel scientific ecosystems", which merges medical science liaison engagement, peer-to-peer education, emerging media and more into a conjoined “ecosystem.” The cross-functional alignment and synergy function, meanwhile, will guide patient-centered educational strategies, while "next-generation measurement" pledges to move beyond standard metrics such as impressions and sends to instead focus on “proprietary, autonomous frameworks” that track behavioral shifts and impacts, according to CMI. 

The business unit's capabilities also include AI-enhanced scientific intelligence, which will deploy “ethical, purpose-built” AI to identify audiences and deliver timely educational exchanges. 

Heading up the buisiness is specialty communications group president Eugene Lee. A decades-long mainstay within CMI leadership, Lee previously held the chief operating officer title before the organizational change. New to the group, however, is Mike Reynolds, who will now serve as SVP, medical and scientific communications. 

Together, the duo will leverage their “specialized domain expertise” to guide the mission, CMI said. 

Related

CMI adopts orphan drug field with dedicated center of excellence

“Medical Affairs is experiencing a monumental evolution. The landscape demands a level of sophistication, omnichannel continuity, and measurement rigor that legacy models simply were not built to support,” Lee explained in the release. “By adapting modern data, AI, and strategic frameworks specifically to the strict compliance and governance needs of Medical Affairs, we are helping biopharma leaders reshape this pillar into a strategic powerhouse.” 

This, Reynolds added, will give medical affairs teams the “strategic leverage they have earned.”

CMI is WPP’s dedicated healthcare media agency and offers solutions in omnichannel activation, audience intelligence, media strategy and more. With the addition of the new unit, the company will focus its practices on medical affairs, scientific communications, rare disease, payer and market access and account-based marketing, it noted in the release. 

Like most media agencies, CMI has been tuned in to the growing wave of AI innovation across the industry. Earlier this summer, the company launched advertising technology division Ad Astra, which centralizes technology solutions through a “modular suite of interoperable solutions that combine precision data, advanced ad tech, and intelligent orchestration capabilities to drive measurable business outcomes,” CMI said at the time.

data.title: Pharma brands dominated last NFL advertising season: report
data.description:
Under embargo: Sept 2 8:00am EST

Kick-off for the 2027-2028 NFL football season is approaching, and with it will come a new slate of winners and losers in the pharma ad space. Ahead of the upcoming season, TV outcomes company EDO is looking back with its NFL TV outcomes report for 2025-2026, ranking the pharma companies and brands that made it to the end zone with high audience engagement scores.  

With millions of Americans tuning in each week to catch the latest football game, it’s been well-established that the NFL ad space is a lucrative slot for marketing across industries. To put it into context, one single NFL ad last season generated the same total impact as about 73 ads during the average primetime broadcast and cable program, EDO pointed out in its new report, released Sept. 2.  EDO measures TV outcomes by analyzing consumer engagement through actions such as branded searchers and website visits. 

During the most recent season, pharma ads stood out among an array of different brand categories that crowded the NFL airwaves during commercial break.

Three out of the top five advertisers for last regular NFL season were pharma brands in Galderma’s skin disease biologic Nemluvio, Novartis’ Pluvicto and Eli Lilly’s Ebyglass. Nemluvio and Pluvicto in particular nabbed the top two spots overall for ad effectiveness across all advertisers, with Nemluvo named the top NFL regular season advertiser overall. 

Brands and products in the top five were 95% more effective during regular-season games than they were during primetime broadcast and cable spots, EDO explained. According to the outcomes company, Nemluvio’s NFL ads were 1,683% more effective than the average regular-season advertiser, while Pluvicto was 780% more effective. 

Top performer Nemluvio had more per-person and per-second engagement than the average ad during the season and marks a new entrant to EDO’s yearly ad effectiveness rating. Ebyglass and Johnson & Johnson’s atypical antipsychotic Caplyta were also new to the top ten, as were Amgen’s Otezla, Lilly’s Zepbound, telehealth company Ro and OTC sleeping med Nyquil. Other mainstays, such as Johnson & Johnson’s Tremfya and AbbVie’s Skyrizi, were bumped down by the new arrivals.

Still, pharma and OTC brands as a category were 95% more effective during NFL airings than they were on primetime broadcast and cable, marking the strongest performance amongst all other categories in EDO’s report.

The most effective pharma ads used key strategies such as using covers of well-known songs, as Lilly’s Ebglyss did in its “Not Always Obvious” 60-second spot, or highlighting product benefits with a catchy tagline such as Caplyta’s “Let in the Lyte” ads, EDO pointed out. 

“The insights in EDO’s latest TV Outcomes Report reinforce what we see across premium television every year: when brands align with the moments audiences value most, it drives stronger engagement and measurable business outcomes,” Disney Advertising SVP, revenue and yield management Jim Minnich commented in the report. 

Related

Pharma's 2026 Super Bowl ads: Novo's Wegovy pill spot is engagement MVP, while Novartis scores 'likeability' touchdown

Outside of the regular NFL season, pharma ads didn’t take center stage as prominently during the Super Bowl. However, Novo Nordisk’s star-studded Wegovy pill promotion snatched the last spot of the top 10 list, with the ad generating 374% more engagement as the median-performing Super Bowl ad in 2026, EDO found. 

Immediately after the Super Bowl back in February, EDO found that pharma ads captured 9% of overall engagement during the game, a slice comparable to that of the auto industry and the snacks and candy product sector. In a separate analysis after the regular NFL season came to a close, EDO found that pharma brands aired ads a total of 332 times across the season, up 13% from the previous year. 

EDO’s latest report, meanwhile, covers the NFL season as a whole including Super Bowl outcomes.

data.title: Rising Stars: Genentech’s Tiffany William's pivot to pharma
data.description:
Genentech performance marketing engagement lead Tiffany William is a self-proclaimed “newbie” in pharma marketing. 

It was only late last year that the UC San Diego alum pivoted from a six-year career in mobile gaming marketing to the pharma realm. After leaving leading game developer Kabam as a senior growth marketing manager in November 2025, it wasn’t game over for William’s career in marketing. Instead, she landed on a whole new map.

Eager for the opportunity to apply marketing that could impact “even more people,” she took on a position at Genentech as performance marketing engagement lead, a role she’s held for ten months now. Since then, she’s been downloading her gaming marketing chops to apply to the pharma marketing sphere.

“Obviously, the context of the marketing itself is very different, and responsibilities far greater in pharma, but being able to kind of transfer what I learned from gaming into pharma has been really good as well,” she said of her career pivot. 

In a Q&A for Fierce Pharma Marketing’s “Rising Stars” series, William discusses the transition and delves into how she’s bringing a “fail fast, learn fast” mentality to Genentech among efforts to help build out a strong “culture of experimentation” within the company’s marketing department. 

Responses have been edited for length and clarity

FPMK: What inspired you to pursue a career in pharma marketing, and what keeps you motivated in your current role?

It was thoroughly a big change, but it gave me the chance to kind of bring a fresh perspective and some of what I learned in gaming into a much more complex and deeply meaningful industry like pharma. And a big part of what drew me to Genentech and pharma marketing was again the opportunity to use marketing in a way that can touch a lot of people's lives and make a difference in their health. That brought a deeper sense of the purpose of the work itself, and that was definitely something that I didn't get to experience when I was still in gaming. 

What keeps me motivated in my role today at Genentech is the opportunity to scale that thinking of performance marketing. How can we use what we're learning from people's behavior to create more relevant and helpful experiences? So, as performance marketing engagement lead at Genentech, I get to work across the portfolio, connect learnings between brands, and help marketers feel more confident using performance data and applying an experiment and optimization mindset in in their work. So, you'll hear me mentioning the words "optimization" and "experiment" a lot, but I especially enjoy making performance marketing feel less daunting and more fun, approachable, and more creative.

FPMK: What has been the most rewarding or challenging project that you've worked on so far?

I think one of the most rewarding challenges has been helping build a stronger culture of experimentation and optimization across Genentech. It is not a single campaign or a single moment. It has really been about helping marketers feel more confident once again using data, triangulating between data sources, asking questions, testing new ideas, and learning from the results. One mindset that I brought with me from gaming is fail fast, learn fast. 

To me, that does not mean being careless or treating every unexpected result as a failure, but rather it means testing with a clear purpose, understanding what the data are telling us, and applying that learning to our decision making instead of waiting for everything to be perfect. I've brought that mindset to life in a few different ways at Genentech. I host office hours five times a week where marketers can bring real business challenges and have an open, practical conversations about it. I've also developed and led incubators and workshops designed to upscale and inspire over 200 marketers at Genentech. And one of the things that I enjoy the most, I must say, is the breadth of the work. One day, I might be helping an SS marketer think about experiments designed to reach population-based decision makers more effectively. On another, I might work with a patient marketer on identifying opportunities to increase patient engagement. 

So, not one day is the same, and I think that's what keeps my job really exciting. And again, because I work at the portfolio level, I have a bird's eye view of what different brands are testing, what they're learning, and that allows me to spot patterns, connect teams with useful insights, and capture these learnings in case studies that can be shared across the board. And we can share these case studies widely through forums like our town halls or marketing newsletters, so that the learnings don't stay just within one brand or one team. 

At the end of the day, I love being able to recognize and celebrate our marketers on the great work that they're doing. When someone who initially found performance marketing really intimidating because it may work with a lot of different data becomes more excited about the test that they're doing, or they start sharing these learnings with another team—that’s one of the clear signs that our change management is working. The behaviors that we've been encouraging our marketers to do are finally being put in practice, and the impact is finally getting bigger than just one workshop or one initiative.

FPMK: What advice would you give to people who worked in pharma marketing for decades?

Genentech marketer Tiffany William

Before going into the advice itself, I must say, being someone who's only been in pharma less than a year, I still have so much to learn from our veterans, people who have spent decades in pharma marketing. Their understanding of patients, HCPs, brands, and the complexity of our industry is something that is deeply, deeply valuable. 

I learn something new every day from our veterans. But if there is one piece of advice that I could give, it is to keep being curious, even when our experiences have given us strong instincts. Customer behaviors, market dynamics, marketing channels, technology are always changing. Staying curious gives us this chance to question our assumptions, but also to look at similar problems with a fresh lens.

I also think that there is a lot that we can learn from other industries. Pharma, of course, has its own limitations and guardrails that other industries may not have. I mean, I come from gaming, so I'm learning about these intricacies also. But that doesn't mean that we cannot be creative or operate at the cutting edge level. We can look outside pharma for inspiration, and then we'll then adapt these ideas into with the needs to fit these ideas to fit the needs and responsibilities of our industry. 

I would also encourage our experienced marketers and senior marketers to not only share their successes but also what did not work and what they learned from it. I feel like when leaders do that, it kind of sets the tone and also shows the next generation of marketers that experimentation is not about having the perfect idea or having the perfect results. It's about being thoughtful, learning from the data, and continuing to improve. So to me, the most powerful combination is that deep industry knowledge and wisdom paired with a beginner's mindset, where you are confident in what you know, but also remaining curious and open-minded about what the next signal might teach us. 

FPMK: What do you like to do when you're not working?

When I'm not working or when I do have free time, I love spending quality time with my husband as well as our three-year-old mini bernedoodle Kuma. I also enjoy going to concerts and planning our next vacation, whether it's a local getaway or international adventure. Honestly, sometimes planning the trip is almost as fun as taking it for me, and those are the things that I like to do that help me recharge and come back to work more energized.

data.title: Bausch + Lomb survey reveals low dry eye awareness
data.description:
Bausch + Lomb is flagging dry eye disease as one of the least recognized symptoms present in perimenopausal and postmenopausal women.

That’s according to the results of the 2026 Bausch + Lomb (Peri)Menopause Survey, which was undertaken by market research platform Suzy among 402 women ages 30-80-plus who are perimenopausal, menopausal or postmenopausal.

It showed that just 14% of perimenopausal and postmenopausal women recognize dry eye as a menopause-related symptom. This contrasts with the 79% who recognize hot flashes.

The survey also found that 78% of those women “were surprised to learn that dry eye is a symptom of perimenopause or menopause,” according to the report.

The survey also showed how this impacted women’s daily lives. This includes more than half (58%) saying they had difficulty reading, while 53% reported difficulty using screens.

Just over a quarter (26%) said they had trouble driving because of the disorder. 

“Given how frequently dry eye symptoms are overlooked during perimenopause and menopause, these findings are an important reminder that eye health deserves to be part of the conversation,” said optometrist Neda Gioia in a release.  

“Recognizing symptoms early can help women seek appropriate care and explore management options that may improve comfort and quality of life.”

Dry eye disease is a common yet underdiagnosed condition affecting some 150 million U.S. adults.

Related

Verily Me, Bausch + Lomb visualize dry eye education in new collaboration

Bausch + Lomb markets Xiidra, a lymphocyte function-associated antigen-1 (LFA-1) antagonist, and Miebo, a semifluorinated alkane, as eye drop treatments for dry eye. 

Sales have scaled up rapidly for Miebo, reaching $410 million in 2025. In the first half of this year, Miebo generated revenue of $167 million, compared to $173 million for Xiidra. The pair’s combined sales were up 27% in the first half compared to the first half of 2025.

But it’s not all been good news. Bausch + Lomb recently came up short in a phase 2 trial that was testing a combination Xiidra and Miebo. Despite missing its primary endpoint, the company said it would be pushing the combo into phase 3. 

This survey comes after personalized AI health app Verily Me teamed up with Bausch + Lomb on boosting education around dry eye disease. Through Verily Me’s digital platform, the partners offer expanded information about dry eye disease risk factors, symptoms, and treatment options, with new content that launched on the app back in June.

Last year, the company also ran a new awareness push dubbed “Eyes Tell the Story: The Impact of Dry Eye.”  That campaign focused on sharing the stories of real people living with dry eye disease.

data.title: Emergent spreads overdose awareness campaign across US, Canada
data.description:
Narcan maker Emergent BioSolutions is joining in on International Overdose Awareness Day by re-upping its "Ready to Rescue" campaign across U.S. college campuses—as well as spreading the message to Canada with a pro athlete partnership. 

The company’s Ready to Rescue push first launched back in 2023 to dismantle stigmas around opioid use and accidental overdose by fostering open dialogs and encouraging preparedness with Emergent’s overdose reversal spray Narcan. With opioids linked to nearly 80% of drug-related deaths worldwide, according to the World Health Organization, the company is now returning to college campuses to reinforce the campaign in partnership with Release Recovery and its CEO Zac Clark. 

Emergent will promote the Ready to Rescue messaging at college campuses across the U.S. this fall, enlisting Clark to share his personal story with opioid dependencies and encourage the younger generation to carry Narcan nasal spray. 

“Today is a reminder of the lives lost to opioid overdoses and serves as a key moment to stand with the families, friends and communities affected by this ongoing public health crisis,” Emergent’s SVP, head of products business, global government and public affairs Paul Williams said in a company release. “While progress has been made, more work remains. By expanding access, awareness and availability to Narcan Nasal Spray 4 mg and Kloxxado Nasal Spray 8 mg we can help more people recognize an opioid emergency and be prepared to act when every second counts.”

Related

Emergent taps ex-NFL star to bring opioid message to college football tailgate parties

Over in Canada, where naloxone nasal spray has long been available without a prescription, the opioid crisis continues with an average of 15 deaths each year due to opioid poisonings, Emergent cited. To address the Canadian public health crisis, the Narcan maker is teaming up with Toronto Blue Jays baseball player Davis Schneider, who shares his story of his late brother to raise awareness and emphasize the importance of carrying Narcan. 

“Being prepared to act in a moment of crisis can mean the difference between life and loss,” Schneider commented. The athlete also took part in Emergent’s “Countermeasures” podcast series to further educate the public on opioid overdose risks. 

Emergent’s Narcan spray became the first FDA-approved over-the-counter naloxone product in 2023, with higher-dose Kloxxado joining its portfolio of emergency drugs last year through a deal with Hikma Pharmaceuticals. Narcan’s over-the-counter availability has been said to have contributed to U.S. annual declines in opioid overdose, according to Emergent. 

The company's campaign website features educational resources on Narcan use during opioid emergencies, including a video explainer from campaign ambassador Emmitt Smith, a former NFL star. Emergent also highlights risk factors and statistics on opioid overdoses in the U.S., urging visitors to “help break the stigma and be ready to rescue.” Smith previously contributed to the campaign by visiting college football tailgates across the U.S. to spread the word alongside Emergent. 

Also on International Overdose Awareness Day, Canada’s government awarded Emergent a standing offer to supply Narcan for three years from the fall of 2026 to the same period in 2029, with an option to extend for an additional two years. The arrangement follows a previous five-year standing offer that will expire this September.

Maryland-based Emergent, which also makes other medicines in the emergency preparedness vein such as an antiviral for smallpox and an inhalation for anthrax exposure, recently slimmed down through another restructuring round that looks to save $40 million in annual costs. The cost-savings push comes as new competitors hit the naloxone field, pressuring Emergent’s Narcan, with second-quarter sales falling 22% year-over-year to $52.4 million,

data.title: Lonza enlists returning exec for new commercial chief post
data.description:
CDMO Lonza is strengthening its market leadership with a newly created role that puts seasoned exec Samanta Cimitan, Ph.D., at the helm of the Swiss manufacturer's commercial operations. 

After a few years away, Cimitan is rejoining Lonza to this time serve as its chief commercial officer, SVP and member of the company’s extended executive committee, effective Jan. 1, 2027. In the new role, she will head up Lonza’s strategic enterprise account management, global marketing and commercial excellence, the CDMO announced in an Aug. 26 press release. 

Through these responsibilities, Lonza looks to better facilitate customer engagement and create a “unified go-to-market approach” across its One Lonza strategy, it said. 

“Samanta’s appointment to the new role of Chief Commercial Officer is another important step in building One Lonza and making the full power of the Lonza Engine work for our partners in the pharmaceutical industry,” Lonza’s CEO, Wolfgang Wienand, explained in the release. “Our ambition is clear: Every customer should benefit from the unique breadth of our science, technology and manufacturing capabilities, helping them translate their breakthrough innovations into viable therapies for patients worldwide.”

Related

Lonza expands partnership with US drugmaker, boosts capacity for ADCs

Wienand attributed the appointment in part to Cimitan’s “CDMO expertise, commercial leadership experience and first-hand knowledge of Lonza,” giving her the chops to foster value “across the full development and manufacturing journey.” 

Cimitan comes back to the Lonza ship after a four-year stint at Celonic Group, a pure play Swiss biologics CDMO. After initially joining as chief business officer, the exec has served as Celonic’s CEO since 2023 and will step down toward the end of this year. She leaves the company having built out a “strong platform for sustainable growth,” Celonic said in a recent release. 

Before transitioning to Celonic, Cimitan spent nearly 13 years in leadership positions at Lonza, starting off in the commercial sector in 2009 and ending as VP of group operations in strategic programs and transformation. Her return comes as Lonza continues to build on its One Lonza strategy, focusing on uniting its core competencies to generate long-term value. 

Earlier this summer, the growing CDMO strengthened its foothold in the lucrative antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) market with a manufacturing expansion that adds new capacity to an existing plant to bring in additional payload-linker production. Over the first half of 2026, Lonza pulled down sales of 3.4 billion Swiss francs ($4.2 billion), marking 16% growth that reflected “continued robust demand” across technologies and “resilience against a backdrop of evolving macroeconomic dynamics,” it said.
